newsitem.title: UK: ROWING-WOMEN MAKE A SPLASH AT HENLEY -- OFFICIALLY.
newsitem.headline: ROWING-WOMEN MAKE A SPLASH AT HENLEY -- OFFICIALLY.

text.p: World class women rowers provided the focus at the traditionally all-male Henley Royal Regatta on Thursday as the first round of the newly-created Princess Royal Cup got underway.

The decision in 1996 by the Stewards, the all-male committee who run the regatta, to make a women's sculling event a permanent part of the Henley programme marked the arrival of women in a sport where they have traditionally been the poor relations.
This year will be the first the event is known by the official title of the Princess Royal Cup and the winner will be presented with a silver cup bought for the event's coming of age.
Thursday's preliminary rounds saw British international Guin Batten, fifth in the 1996 Olympic Games, and Swedish arch-rival Maria Brandin, fourth, pass effortlessly through their qualifying races.
The two are on track for a showdown in Sunday's final -- a prospect which Batten relishes.
"The most important thing is to take one race at a time at Henley because in one-on-one racing you can never be sure, but I would like to meet Maria in the final."
Brandin is the current sculling world champion and won the women's sculling event at Henley last year. Each has won two of their four meetings this year.
In 1993 women raced over the full course at the Henley Regatta for the first time. But it was only in 1996 that a women's event became a permanent addition to the racing programme.
"I am proud to be part of the tradition of Henley and it would be good to see more women's events coming in," Batten said.
Further rounds of the Diamond sculls saw Scotland's Peter Haining, three times world lightweight sculling champion, move through to the next round, beating Australian Nick McDonald-Crowley.

Also racing on Friday in the Diamonds will be Britain's Greg Searle, 1992 Olympic gold and 1996 Olympic bronze medallist, though not in sculling events, and American Jamie Koven, formerly of the United States national eight.

Showing their form for the first time at Henley in the coxless pairs event and winning comfortably were British internationals Ben Hunt-Davies and Robert Thatcher, who train at Leander Club, the same breeding ground as Olympic gold medallists Steve Redgrave and Matthew Pinsent.
Redgrave and Pinsent dominated the pairs event for years, winning the Henley event four times out of the last six.
